chapter: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
title: Saxophone as a new instrument; violinists turning to reeds
summary: They talk about Paul Beesey, Weedhoff and the Six Brown Brothers, why saxophone was easy, and why violinists took up reeds.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, I think also somewhere there's a story that Bud was impressed by Beesey. So you've mentioned. He might have. Bud, Beesey, the sparkling ivory keys and the shiny horn and some of those things I think have come out in later years as a possible influence on Bud.
Also, Beesey had a fantastic slap tongue, and that always intrigued any saxophone player.
There have been some Columbia records, Paul Beesey's trio. Do you happen to know who the other people are? No, I've got the records.
Was Weedhoff of any importance? Was it a saxophone player in that period?

You know, the saxophone at that point was really a quite new instrument. I mean, it wasn't recognized by legitimate musicians at all. And I think the first impression any of us had of a saxophone came either from Weedhoff or from the Six Brown Brothers.

And it was a fascinating instrument. It was an incredible number of keys on it. And also the fact that it's a remarkably easy one to play. Not well, but you can certainly play it very easily compared to a clarinet, for instance.

Strange how many violinists, when the music picture changed, went to a Reed instrument. Do you think it had anything to do with the range being comparable? They went to clarinet frequently, or went to alto.
Or was it just the fact that this was a new opening?
The horn players had already monopolized the horn business.
Also, the horn's a terribly difficult thing. Yeah. You almost have to start it before you're bright enough to realize how hard it is. I've told this to my partner. It's not going to get very well.
Too easy to become discouraged. Yeah.

When I say a saxophone is being much more easy than a clarinet, it's because both octaves are in the same key. You push an octave shift, and you're still in business. And the clarinet, you've got that difficult transition because the lower octave and the upper are in different keys. Oh, yes.
Bud fooled around with the clarinet, too. You think that came later?
